items.stem: State the reagent that the gas released from a carbonate sample is bubbled through.
items.modelAnswer: Limewater.

items.stem: State the positive result of the carbonate ion test.
items.modelAnswer: The limewater turns cloudy.

items.stem: Explain why the limewater turns cloudy during the carbonate test.
items.modelAnswer: Because a white precipitate of calcium carbonate forms in the limewater — the suspended calcium carbonate is the cloudiness.

items.stem: Sodium carbonate reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid. State the two products formed other than the salt sodium chloride.
items.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide and water — the ionic equation is CO3 2- (aq) + 2H+ (aq) → CO2 (g) + H2O (l).

items.stem: State the colour of the precipitate that identifies iodide ions in the halide test.
items.modelAnswer: Yellow — silver iodide is the yellow precipitate.

items.stem: State the acid used to acidify the sample before silver nitrate is added.
items.modelAnswer: Nitric acid.

items.stem: Explain why the negative ions of the Group 7 elements are called halide ions.
items.modelAnswer: Because they are the negative ions formed by the Group 7 elements, the halogens — a halide is a halogen's negative ion.

items.stem: Three unknown solutions each give a precipitate with silver nitrate after nitric acid: one white, one cream and one yellow. State the halide ion present in each.
items.modelAnswer: White = chloride (silver chloride), cream = bromide (silver bromide), yellow = iodide (silver iodide).

items.stem: State the formula of the sulfate ion.
State the positive result of the sulfate ion test.
items.modelAnswer: A white precipitate of barium sulfate forms.

items.stem: Explain why barium nitrate solution can replace barium chloride solution in the sulfate test.
items.modelAnswer: Because either barium salt provides the barium ions needed to form the white barium sulfate precipitate.

items.stem: After acidifying a solution with hydrochloric acid and adding barium chloride, a student sees no precipitate. State whether sulfate ions are present in the solution.
items.modelAnswer: No — a white precipitate of barium sulfate forms if the sulfate ion is present, so no precipitate means the sulfate ion is absent.

items.stem: State the acid-base character of metal oxides.
items.modelAnswer: Metal oxides are basic.

items.stem: State how many outer-shell electrons a non-metal atom holds.
items.modelAnswer: Four to seven (metals hold one to three).

items.stem: Explain why the electrical conductivity test is decisive when sorting metals from non-metals.
items.modelAnswer: Because metals conduct well while non-metals are poor conductors, so a conductivity reading separates the two classes cleanly.

items.stem: The oxide of element X dissolves in water and the solution turns universal indicator purple, well above pH 7. State the acid-base character of X's oxide and the class of element X.
items.modelAnswer: The oxide is basic (alkaline), so X is a metal — metal oxides are basic.

items.stem: State which side of the periodic table the non-metals occupy.
items.modelAnswer: The right-hand side — metals sit on the left.

items.stem: State which class of element makes up the vast majority of the periodic table.
items.modelAnswer: The metals.

items.stem: Explain why elements bordering the zig-zag line are hard to classify as simply metal or non-metal.
items.modelAnswer: Because elements bordering that line show traits of both sides — they are the semi-metals, or metalloids.

items.stem: A newly discovered element is placed three columns in from the right-hand edge of the periodic table, clear of the zig-zag line. State its class using its position alone.
items.modelAnswer: A non-metal — on the periodic table metals sit on the left and non-metals on the right, so position is itself the classifier.

items.stem: State the value of the Avogadro constant.
items.modelAnswer: 6.02 × 10^23 particles per mole.

items.stem: State what the molar mass of an element matches, in grams.
items.modelAnswer: The relative atomic mass (Ar) — the mass of one mole of the element in grams.

items.stem: Explain why one mole of carbon and one mole of helium contain the same number of particles.
items.modelAnswer: Because equal amounts in moles contain equal numbers of particles, whatever the substance — the mole counts particles, it does not weigh them.

items.stem: A student needs the molar mass of carbon dioxide, CO2 (Ar: C = 12, O = 16). State how it is found from the atomic masses.
items.modelAnswer: Add the atomic masses of all the atoms in the formula together: 12 + (2 × 16) = 44 g/mol, matching the relative formula mass.

items.stem: State the relationship linking moles, mass and molar mass.
items.modelAnswer: moles = mass ÷ molar mass — the mass divided by the molar mass.

items.stem: State the rearranged relationship used to find the mass from a known number of moles.
items.modelAnswer: mass = moles × molar mass — the moles multiplied by the molar mass.

items.stem: Explain why molar mass is measured in g mol^-1.
items.modelAnswer: Because molar mass is the mass of one mole — a mass per amount of substance — so its unit is grams per mole, g mol^-1.

items.stem: A student has 0.500 mol of water, H2O (Mr = 18). State the mass of the sample.
items.modelAnswer: mass = moles × molar mass = 0.500 × 18 = 9.0 g.
